Title: Uncovering Safety Risks of Large Language Models through Concept Activation Vector

In this paper, the authors aim to address the safety risks of large language models (LLMs) by developing a novel attack method that can generate both embedding-level and prompt-level attacks with automatically selected perturbation hyperparameters. The authors introduce a Safety Concept Activation Vector (SCA V) framework, which accurately interprets LLMs' safety mechanisms and eliminates potential misleading heuristics of existing attack baselines. The proposed attack method significantly improves the attack success rate and response quality while requiring less training data. The authors also unveil the safety risks and mechanisms of diverse LLMs by applying their attack method, discovering that their safety issues are severe. The paper provides valuable insights into the safety mechanism of LLMs and highlights the need for further safety alignment works to prevent the misuse of these powerful models.

The paper "Uncovering Safety Risks of Large Language Models through Concept Activation Vector" by Zhihao Xu, Ruixuan Huang, Changyu Chen, Shuai Wang, and Xiting Wang presents a novel approach to attacking large language models (LLMs) by exploiting their safety mechanisms. The authors propose a Safety Concept Activation Vector (SCA V) framework, which accurately interprets LLMs' safety mechanisms and guides the attack process. The SCA V framework is used to develop an SCA V-guided attack method that can generate both embedding-level and prompt-level attacks with automatically selected perturbation hyperparameters. The authors evaluate their attack method on several open-source LLMs and demonstrate significant improvements in attack success rate and response quality compared to existing methods. Additionally, they find that their generated attack prompts may be transferable to GPT-4, and the embedding-level attacks may also be transferred to other white-box LLMs. The paper highlights the safety risks present in current LLMs and provides insights into their safety mechanisms.

The authors' contributions include the establishment of the SCA V framework, the development of the SCA V-guided attack method, and the evaluation of their method on several LLMs. The SCA V framework accurately models LLMs' safe mechanisms and provides a principled optimization goal for finding high-quality embedding- and prompt-level attacks. The SCA V-guided attack method eliminates the need for time-consuming hyperparameter tuning and provides a closed-form solution for the optimal perturbation magnitudes and layer selection. The authors' approach significantly improves ASR, language quality, response usefulness, and reduces the training data required.

The paper also reveals the safety risks and mechanisms of diverse LLMs by applying the attack method. The authors discover that even seemingly well-aligned LLMs like LLaMA-2 provide relevant answers to a significant percentage of malicious instructions, and the attacks of one LLM can be transferred to others, including black-box ones like GPT-4. The paper highlights the potential dangers of LLMs and the need for further research to address these safety risks.

Sure, here is the summary for the "Introduction to the Mechanism of Success" section:

The rapid advancement in large language models (LLMs) has raised concerns about their potential misuse. To address these concerns, researchers have conducted extensive safety alignment works to prevent LLMs from being exploited for harmful activities. However, various attack methods have been discovered that can reverse these safety alignment efforts. These attacks can identify vulnerabilities in safety alignment technologies and enable developers to fix them promptly, reducing the societal safety risks of LLMs.

Existing attack methods utilize different levels of information from LLMs to achieve varying degrees of model understanding and control. However, their attack success rates are constrained by an insufficient understanding of LLMs' internal working mechanisms. Some recent attack works further utilize model embeddings at intermediate layers, which can achieve significantly higher attack success rates on white-box LLMs. However, these methods cannot be applied to black-box APIs and may result in low-quality responses.

To address these issues, we propose a Safety Concept Activation Vector (SCA V) framework that accurately interprets LLMs' safety mechanisms and guides the subsequent attack process. Our SCA V-guided attack method utilizes SCA V to design principled optimization goals for finding high-quality embedding- and prompt-level attacks. Our method significantly improves attack success rates and response quality while requiring less training data. We also unveil the safety risks and mechanisms of diverse LLMs by applying our attack method. Our results show that even seemingly well-aligned LLMs provide relevant answers to a significant percentage of malicious instructions, and the attacks of one LLM can be transferred to others, including black-box ones like GPT-4.

Overall, our work aims to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the safety risks of LLMs and to develop more effective attack methods to address these risks. Our proposed SCA V framework and SCA V-guided attack method offer a principled approach to improving the attack success rates and response quality of LLMs, while also providing insights into the safety mechanisms and risks of these models.

Related Work
========

Existing work on uncovering the safety risks of large language models (LLMs) has primarily focused on developing attack methods that exploit vulnerabilities in the models' safety alignment mechanisms. These attacks have been shown to be effective in manipulating the models' behavior and eliciting harmful responses. However, these attacks have limitations, such as requiring manually designed prompts or relying on heuristics to identify vulnerable dimensions in the models' embeddings.

Our work builds upon and extends these previous efforts by introducing a Safety Concept Activation Vector (SCA V) framework, which accurately interprets LLMs' safety mechanisms and guides the attack process. Our SCA V-guided attack method improves the attack success rate and response quality while automatically selecting hyperparameters and supporting both embedding- and prompt-level attacks.

We evaluate our attack method on several open-source LLMs and demonstrate its effectiveness in generating high-quality attacks that can be applied in both black-box and white-box scenarios. Our experiments also reveal the safety risks present in current LLMs, such as their ability to provide relevant answers to a high percentage of malicious instructions.

Overall, our work provides a more comprehensive understanding of the safety risks of LLMs and demonstrates the effectiveness of our SCA V-guided attack method in uncovering these risks.
